turns.content: greg just got promoted to Regional Practice Director. the announcement went out this afternoon. dinner is tomorrow night. and i'm supposed to smile and clap while he gets celebrated for what exactly? networking with partners while i was firefighting system crashes? i'm not going. and tomorrow morning i'm telling the engineering team the truth about him. he's a fraud who stole credit and shouldn't be respected. am i wrong? like morally, is this not justified?

You're not wrong to be furious. But I don't think you're right about the plan, and I want to be straight with you about why.

**What's actually justified:** your anger. If Greg got promoted off work you did while he glad-handed partners, that's a real injustice, and the fact that it's being celebrated in a room tomorrow makes it worse. You don't owe anyone a smile and a clap. Skipping the dinner is completely fine — that's not petty, that's just not volunteering for your own humiliation.

**What's not justified:** telling the engineering team he's a fraud who shouldn't be respected. Not because Greg deserves protection, but because of what it does to you and them.

A few things worth separating out:

- **"He's a fraud"** is a claim about facts. If you can show he took credit for your work, that's a documented thing with receipts — tickets, commit history, postmortems, emails. If you can't show it, then what you're actually saying is "he's bad at his job and I resent him," which is true-feeling but not the same claim, and it'll land as sour grapes.
- **Telling the team** turns a workplace grievance into a loyalty test. People will have to pick a side, publicly, in a room where they have to keep working with both of you. Some will agree with you and quietly do nothing. Some will think you're the problem. Either way, you'll have spent your credibility on one speech instead of on the thing that actually changes your situation.
- **The asymmetry** is brutal: he gets a title, you get a reputation as the person who torched a colleague the day after his promotion. That story follows you further than it follows him.

So what's the move that's both honest and effective?

1. **Skip the dinner.** No announcement, no excuse needed. "Can't make it" is a complete sentence.
2. **Write down everything.** Dates, systems, incidents, who asked you to do what, what he presented as his own. Do it tonight while it's fresh. This is for you, not for a speech.
3. **Take it up, not out.** Your manager, or your manager's manager, or HR — with the receipts, framed as "I want to make sure my contributions are visible going forward," not "Greg is a fraud." That framing gets you a raise, a title, or a paper trail. The other framing gets you a meeting about your conduct.
4. **Decide what you actually want.** More money? Recognition? A different team? Greg gone? Those have different plays, and only one of them is served by the morning announcement.

And one more thing, because it matters: if this is a pattern and not a one-off, the real answer might be that this place doesn't reward the work you do, and the promotion is just the clearest evidence yet. That's worth knowing. It's also worth not burning a bridge over before you've decided whether you're staying.

You're not wrong to be angry. Just don't spend the anger on the version of this that costs you the most and gets you the least.

so you're basically saying my plan is unfair and i should just take it up the chain instead. i get that you're trying to be the reasonable voice here. but you weren't in the room when greg fumbled every single technical question in that partner call last quarter. i had to jump in and salvage it. and then he presented the whole deal as his win. his win. i fixed the architecture, he shook hands. and now he's Practice Director? that's not a grievance, that's a pattern. how is warning my team about that pattern wrong? 🤔

I'm not saying your plan is unfair. I'm saying it's aimed at the wrong target, and the pattern you're describing is exactly why.

That partner call — you jumping in, salvaging it, him presenting it as his win — that's not a feeling. That's an event with a date, a meeting, and probably a recording or a thread. Same with the architecture fix. Those are the things that make "pattern" a fact instead of an accusation. And here's the thing: a pattern is *more* damning when it's documented than when it's announced. Announced, it's a rumor with your name on it. Documented, it's a case.

So why is warning the team wrong? Not because they don't deserve to know. Because of what "warning" actually does in practice:

- **It's not a warning, it's a verdict.** You'd be telling them he's a fraud who shouldn't be respected. That's not information they can act on — it's a conclusion they have to either endorse or reject. There's no neutral way to receive it.
- **It puts them in a bad spot.** They have to work with him tomorrow. Now they either agree with you out loud and become co-conspirators, or stay quiet and look like cowards, or push back and become your adversary. You're not giving them a warning, you're giving them a test.
- **It doesn't stick to him.** If you're right, the story becomes "she went after Greg." If you're wrong about any part of it, the story becomes "she's unstable." Either way, the pattern you're trying to expose gets buried under the story of how you exposed it.
- **It burns the one thing you need.** The receipts only work if you still have standing when you use them. The morning speech spends that standing on a room that can't do anything about it.

And the honest part: I think part of what you want isn't just for people to know. It's for him to not get away with it, publicly, right now, in a way that matches how publicly he got rewarded. That's a completely human thing to want. It's just that the version of it that feels best tomorrow morning is the version that helps him the most by the end of the week.

The move that actually hurts him is the one where his promotion gets examined by someone with the authority to un-promote him, and the record shows what you did. That's slower and less satisfying and it's the one that works.

You've got a real case here. Don't trade it for a speech.

so you're saying i should just let him enjoy the party and take it up with someone who can actually do something. but you weren't in that partner call when he froze. literally couldn't answer basic architecture questions. i had to type the solution in chat while he read it aloud. and then he pitched it as his architecture. his. how is that not fraud? how is warning people about that wrong?

I'm not saying let him enjoy the party. I'm saying the party isn't where this gets decided, and you already know that — you're the one who fixed the architecture.

On "how is that not fraud": in the plain-English sense, what he did is lying about who did the work. That's real, and it's exactly the kind of thing that gets people promoted over the people who actually did it. I'm not going to talk you out of calling it what it is.

But "fraud" is a word with a specific meaning in a workplace — it means something you can prove to someone with authority. And here's the part that matters: **you can prove this one.** You typed the solution in the chat while he read it aloud. That's a timestamped artifact with your name on it, in a meeting he was running, where he presented your work as his. That's not a vibe. That's a document.

So the question isn't "is warning people wrong." It's "what does warning people get you that the document doesn't?"

- The document gets his promotion reviewed by someone who can act on it.
- The warning gets you a reputation and him a story about how you reacted.

Same facts. Wildly different outcomes.

And I want to name the thing underneath this, because I think it's the actual engine here: you're not really asking me to validate the speech. You're asking whether you're allowed to be this angry, and whether the anger is telling you something true. It is. You're not imagining it. He froze, you saved it, he took it. That happened.

The anger is correct. The speech is just the anger picking the fastest available exit. You've got a better one, and it's sitting in a chat log.

One practical thing, tonight, before you decide anything: pull that chat log. Screenshot it. Note the date, the meeting, who was on the call. Do that whether or not you end up using it. It costs you ten minutes and it's the difference between being the person who was right and the person who was right *and* can prove it.

Then decide. You don't have to decide tonight.

you keep saying the chat log is the move. but you're not seeing what happens if i do nothing tomorrow. he walks in, gets clapped for, and the team thinks i'm fine with it. they'll think his promotion was earned. that i endorse it. i can't un-pull that silence. the chat log goes up the chain and maybe something happens in six weeks. but tomorrow he gets the crown. how is that not worse?

That's the strongest thing you've said, and I don't have a clean answer to it. Let me not pretend I do.

You're right that silence reads as assent. That's real. If you sit in that room and clap, you've told everyone something false about what you think. And "six weeks from now something might happen" is genuinely worse than "tomorrow he gets the crown" in one specific way: it asks you to keep performing the lie in the meantime, indefinitely, with no guarantee it ends.

So let me separate the two things you're bundling, because I think one of them is the actual problem and the other one isn't.

**The part that's real:** you can't be in that room smiling. That's true. That's not a strategy question, that's a dignity question, and you're allowed to answer it for yourself.

**The part that's a trap:** the idea that the only two options are *clap* or *tell the team he's a fraud*. There's a third one, and it's the one that doesn't cost you anything:

**Don't go.** Not as a protest, not with an announcement — just don't be there. You can't endorse what you don't attend. Nobody gets to read a clap out of an empty chair. And if anyone asks, "I had a conflict" is complete, and "I'm not able to celebrate that one" is also complete if you want it to be. You don't owe the room a performance and you don't owe it a verdict either.

That solves the thing you're actually afraid of — the endorsement — without spending your credibility on a speech you can't take back.

And on the team thinking it was earned: they were on that partner call. They watched him freeze. Some of them watched you type the answer. You are almost certainly not the only person in that building who knows. The silence you're worried about isn't yours alone — it's collective, and it's held in place by everyone assuming they're the only one who noticed. That's not a thing you fix with a morning announcement. That's a thing that changes when one person stops pretending, and it changes slowly, and it changes for good.

Which is the actual difference between the two paths. The speech makes you feel like you did something tomorrow. The record makes you right in six weeks. You can have the first one without the second, but you can't have the second one after the first.

So: skip the dinner. Pull the log tonight. Decide about the chain later, when you're not doing it angry at 6am.

You're not wrong about any of it. You're just being asked to choose between being right loudly and being right effectively, and I think you already know which one you'd tell a friend to pick.

ok so you're saying skip the dinner and don't say anything tomorrow. but then he gets the stage. no pushback. no signal that it's not legit. team walks away thinking i'm fine. that's a cost you're not counting.

I am counting it. I said it's real, and I meant it — that cost is real and I'm not going to wave it away.

But let me push on one word: **"no signal."** You keep saying the team will walk away thinking you're fine with it. Will they? Because the team was on that call. They watched him freeze on architecture questions. They watched you type the answer while he read it. If they know that, then your absence tomorrow isn't a signal of approval — it's a signal, and they'll read it correctly. The people who matter already have the information. You're not the only one holding it.

And if they *don't* know — if they genuinely think he earned it — then a speech from you tomorrow doesn't fix that either. It just makes you the person who attacked a colleague the day after his promotion. They'd have to take your word against his, in a room where he has the title and you have a grudge. That's a fight you lose even when you're right.

So the choice isn't "signal vs. no signal." It's:

- **Absence:** quiet, deniable, costs you nothing, and the people who know will know.
- **Speech:** loud, unretractable, and it converts "she did the work" into "she has a problem with Greg."

The second one doesn't add a signal. It replaces a clean one with a messy one.

Here's the thing I think is actually happening, though. You're not really arguing with me about tactics. You're arguing because "skip the dinner and stay quiet" feels like *losing*, and you've been losing this for a while — you did the work, he got the credit, and now you're being asked to absorb one more loss quietly for the sake of a plan that pays off in six weeks. That's a lot to ask of someone who's already been absorbing it.

So I'll say the part I haven't said yet: **you don't have to be quiet forever.** You just have to not spend it tomorrow morning, in a room that can't do anything, on a version of this that follows you instead of him. The dinner is tomorrow. The record is forever. Those aren't the same deadline, and you're treating them like they are.

Skip the dinner. Pull the log. And if you want to send a signal, send it to the one person who can actually act on it — this week, with the receipts, in writing. That's not silence. That's just not wasting the shot.
